sheng.title: 聖人: not a saint
sheng.body: 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the English word misleads. This is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. It is not only a wise man either. The character has 耳, an ear, and the Shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. This is the figure’s last appearance in the book, and the portrait is plain: no store, open hands, no contest.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 耳部: 聖，通也。从耳呈聲。

xin.title: 信: a person beside their word
xin.body: 信 is 亻, a person, beside 言, speech. The Shuowen calls it a joined-meaning character, 會意, and defines it as 誠, sincerity. The picture is easy to read: a person who stands next to what was said. So 信 is not “true” in the sense of a statement that matches a fact. It is “trustworthy”: words that someone will keep. From it come the senses “to believe”, “good faith”, and later “a letter”, words sent with a person’s name on them. The Laozi uses it often and gives it weight. Where good faith is not enough, there is no faith in return (17, 23). The sage keeps faith with the faithless too, and so gains 信 (49). Light promises bring little trust (63). The last passage opens with it. Before you weigh these words, the text says, ask the first question: can they be relied on?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 言部: 信，誠也。从人从言。會意。

mei.title: A beautiful book warns against beauty
mei.body: 美言不信: beautiful words are not to be trusted. The sentence is itself beautiful. It mirrors the line before it, four characters against four, and the book that it closes is one of the finest pieces of rhymed prose in Chinese. The author knew this. So the first lines can be read as a warning about the book in your hands: you have enjoyed these sayings, and enjoyment is not a reason to rely on them. Passage 62 has the practical side: 美言可以市, “fine words can be taken to market”; another old punctuation reads 美言可以市尊, “fine words can buy honour”. They are a currency. Passage 1 began by saying that a way that can be told is not the constant Dao. Passage 81 ends by saying that words that please are not the ones to trust. Between these two cautions stand five thousand words. Is that a contradiction, or the only honest way to frame a book?

truth-beauty.title: Not “truth” against “beauty”
truth-beauty.body: English readers hear the first lines through a famous pair. Plato distrusted the poets; Keats answered that beauty is truth and truth beauty. The Laozi seems to take a side in that quarrel. It does not, because neither of its words means what ours do. [[信|xin]] is reliability between people, and no abstract Truth stands behind it. 美 is what pleases the senses: the Shuowen defines it by the taste of mutton, and passage 2 says that when all the world knows the beautiful as beautiful, ugliness is already there. So the lines are practical. Words that can be relied on are usually plain, because they were not shaped to please; words shaped to please were shaped for the hearer’s pleasure, and that is a different aim. Passage 35 says of Dao in the mouth: 淡乎其無味, “how bland; it has no taste”.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 羊部: 美，甘也。从羊从大。

form.title: Three mirrors, and a different middle
form.body: The first six lines are three mirror pairs. Each pair has the form A is not B; B is not A: 信 and 美, 善 and 辯, 知 and 博. The figure closes each thought like a clasp, and it makes the lines easy to remember. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts has the pairs in another order and with one different word. It reads: 知者不博，博者不知。善者不多，多者不善, “those who know are not broad; the broad do not know. The good do not have much; those with much are not good.” There is no 辯, no arguing, in that version. In its place is 多, “much”, which leads straight into the next line: the sage does not pile up. The received text’s line about argument may come from another edition or an editor. Both versions exist. The silk one makes the passage a single thought about having little.

bian.title: 辯: speech between two litigants
bian.body: 辯 is built like a courtroom. In the middle is 言, speech. On each side stands 辛. The Shuowen explains the pair 辡 as 辠人相與訟也, “two accused persons who bring suit against each other”, and it says of 辛 that it has to do with offence and punishment. Then 辯 itself: 治也。从言在辡之閒, “to settle; speech placed between the two litigants”. So the word for eloquent argument began as pleading in a lawsuit. To 辯 is to make one’s case against an opponent before a judge. That is the manner that the line rejects: speech as a contest with a winner. Passage 45 says 大辯若訥, “the greatest eloquence seems to stammer”. English “argue” once meant “to make clear”. The Chinese word never lost the two parties and the offence.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 辡部: 辯，治也。从言在辡之閒。 辡，辠人相與訟也。从二辛。

debaters.title: The age of the debaters
debaters.body: In the fourth and third centuries BCE, 辯 was a profession. Rulers kept halls of scholars who argued before them; the king of Qi housed hundreds at the Jixia gate of his capital, with stipends and no duties except to dispute. The Mohists made disputation a method with rules, to fix what is so and what is not so. The debaters around Hui Shi and Gongsun Long argued that a white horse is not a horse, and that there are moments when a flying arrow neither moves nor is at rest. Travelling persuaders talked states into and out of alliances, and one speech could make a man chief minister. Even Mencius, who despised the trade, was accused of it and replied: 予豈好辯哉？予不得已也, “do I love disputation? I have no choice.” Against this background 善者不辯 is not a remark about manners. It declines the main intellectual activity of the time, in a book that never names an opponent.

bo.title: 博: five cartloads of books
bo.body: 博 is breadth. The Shuowen says 大通也, “great and thorough reach”, and the character has 十, ten, the complete number, at its side. For the Confucians it was a duty: the noble person 博學於文, “learns broadly in the records”. The Zhuangzi says of the debater Hui Shi that his books filled five carts, and adds that his way was crooked and his words missed the mark. Books were bundles of bamboo strips then, and five carts were a great library. The Laozi sets 知, knowing, against this. Its own account of knowing is in two earlier lines: 其出彌遠，其知彌少, “the further one goes out, the less one knows” (47); and in learning one gains each day, in Dao one loses each day (48). This is not praise of ignorance. A person can know one thing to the bottom, or many things by their surfaces. Which do you do?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 十部: 博，大通也。从十从尃。尃，布也。

wb-one.title: Wang Bi: three notes of four characters
wb-one.body: Wang Bi’s last comments are as spare as the text. On “words to trust are not beautiful”: 實在質也, “the substance is in the plain stuff”. On “beautiful words are not to be trusted”: 本在樸也, “the root is in the uncarved wood”. On “those who know are not broad”: 極在一也, “the summit is in the One”. Each note has four characters and the same frame: X is in Y. He names three places where the real thing lives: 質, raw material before ornament; 樸, the uncut block, the book’s image for the unworked self since passage 15; and 一, the One of passages 22 and 39. Ornament, carving, and breadth all move away from these. A young man who had read everything wrote these three lines, and he died at twenty-three. He gives no argument for them. Would an argument have helped?

ji.title: 積: grain in a heap
ji.body: 積 has 禾, the grain plant, on its left; the Shuowen defines it 聚也, to gather into a heap. Its right side, 責, gives the sound and is itself the word for a debt that is claimed. The first sense is the stack of sheaves and the full granary. Stores were the strength of a state: the texts of the age measure a ruler by his 積, and a general by how many years of grain stand behind him. The word also had an honoured moral use. The Confucian Xunzi built his teaching on it: heap up earth and you make a mountain; heap up good acts and you make a sage. 聖人不積 answers both. The Zhuangzi’s last chapter sums up the old master in these terms: he took having a store as not having enough. What do you keep in heaps, and against what day?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 禾部: 積，聚也。从禾責聲。
Zhuangzi, “Tianxia” (天下): 以有積為不足

ji-yi.title: 既: already done
ji-yi.body: 既以為人 is four characters: already, using, for, others. 既 marks an act as complete. Most English versions write “the more the sage does for others, the more…”, a sliding scale. The Chinese puts a finished act first: having already done it for others, the sage has still more. As a full verb 既 means “to use up”, as in passage 35, and some readers hear that sense here: having spent everything. The ordinary grammar of 既以 says only “having already”, and our rendering stays with it. 為 is read wèi here, “for the sake of”; in the last line of the book the same character is read wéi, “to act”. 人 and 己 stand side by side: others, self. The sentence has no subject and no “he”; our English leaves a gap before “has” to keep that. And it does not say what was done or given. Goods, strength, teaching, life: the line fits all of them. Which did you supply as you read?

yu.title: 愈: the bellows returns
yu.body: 己愈有, 己愈多: oneself, the more, has; oneself, the more, much. The word 愈, “more and more”, has appeared once before in the book, in the picture of the bellows: 虛而不屈，動而愈出, “empty and never exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out” (5). There the space between heaven and earth is a bellows that gives because it is empty. Here the sage is the same instrument. Nothing is stored inside, and so the flow through does not stop. The claim sounds like a paradox, and people repeat it as a strategy: give, and you will get. The text does not offer that bargain. A person who gives in order to have more is still piling up, by a longer road. The line describes what is observed in one who does not pile up at all. It may be simple arithmetic of another kind: what is used for others is not lost to the user.

wb-give.title: Wang Bi: what all things honour
wb-give.body: On 聖人不積 Wang Bi writes: 無私自有，唯善是與，任物而已。 “The sage has no private holding of their own; gives only where it is good; and leaves things to themselves, that is all.” The middle phrase echoes the end of passage 79, where heaven’s way is always with the good. On “has still more” he adds three characters: 物所尊也, “this is what things honour”. On “has more again”: 物所歸也, “this is what things come home to”. So for Wang Bi the “more” is not more goods. The one who keeps nothing back is honoured by all things and becomes the place to which they return, as the sea is the place to which rivers return. 歸 is his favourite verb for this, and he used it in passage 73: stay low, and things come home. The sage’s wealth is that things return.

li.title: 利: Legge’s “sharpness”
li.body: Legge’s last sentence begins: “With all the sharpness of the Way of Heaven, it injures not”. Other translators write “benefits and does not harm”. Both come from one word. 利 is written with 禾, grain, and 刂, a knife, and its first sense is the keen edge of a blade; the Shuowen defines it as 銛, sharp. From the sharp tool that works well came “advantage, profit, benefit”. Legge chose the older sense, and it gives a striking line: heaven’s way is keen and does not cut. Passage 58 says the same of the sage: square and does not slice, pointed and does not stab. Most readers take the later sense, as we do. The Chinese does not choose. Legge also wrote “sincere” for 信, which makes trust a feeling inside the speaker, and added “(in the Tao)” twice. His very last words are “he does not strive”.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

sheng-dao.title: The sage’s way, or everyone’s?
sheng-dao.body: The received text ends with 聖人之道, “the way of the sage”. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts has one word less: 人之道，為而弗爭, “the way of people: act and do not contend”. The difference is large. In passage 77, 人之道 was the bad way, the one that takes from the poor and offers to the rich, set against heaven’s way. If the silk reading is the older one, the book here gives 人之道 a second meaning: the way that people could walk. It is no longer the special path of a rare figure. It is the human way as such, restored: heaven benefits and does not harm; people act and do not contend. A later hand may have added 聖 to remove the clash with passage 77. Which ending do you prefer: one that describes a sage, or one that describes you?

bu-zheng.title: 爭: the book’s last word
bu-zheng.body: The final character of the received text is 爭, with 不 before it: not contend. The Shuowen defines 爭 in one word, 引也, “to pull”, and the character is commonly explained as two hands, one above and one below, that pull at a single object. It is a tug-of-war. The Shuowen even defines 訟, a lawsuit, by this word. 不爭 runs through the whole book like a thread, and here the thread is tied off. Do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend (3). Water benefits all things and does not contend (8). Because the sage does not contend, no one under heaven can contend with the sage (22, 66). It is the 德 of not contending (68). Heaven’s way does not contend and is good at winning (73). And last: act, and do not contend. The book does not end on Dao, or 德, or 無. It ends on a pair of hands that let go.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 𠬪部: 爭，引也。从𠬪、𠂆。
Shuowen Jiezi, 言部: 訟，爭也。

last-page.title: An ending that was made later
last-page.body: The historian Sima Qian tells that Laozi wrote a book in two parts, of five thousand and some words, and went away; no one knows where he ended. For two thousand years readers have taken this passage as the farewell: a look back at the words, an open hand, and silence. The oldest manuscripts tell another story. In the Mawangdui silk texts this passage is in the middle: it follows our passage 80, which follows our passage 66, and our passage 67 comes next. Their book ends with our passage 37. The Guodian bamboo slips, a century and more older, are reported to lack this passage entirely. So the “last passage” is the work of an editor, perhaps of the early Han. It was a wise choice. A book whose first line doubts the telling ends with a line that doubts fine words, and then stops.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B (order of passages)

plain.title: One plain sentence
plain.body: Today, before you send a message that matters, do the test of the first line. Read what you wrote and mark every phrase that is there to please, to impress, or to protect you. Then ask of what remains: will I stand beside this? That is 信, the person next to the word. Send the short version. Later in the day, when someone says a thing that you think is wrong, try the third line once. Do not argue. Say what you know in one sentence, without the case for it, and stop. Notice the discomfort; the urge to add a second sentence is 辯, the litigant in you. And once, give something away to the end: finish the good coffee on a guest, give the whole afternoon. See whether “has still more” is true in any sense that you can feel.

give-have.title: 與 and 有, 人 and 己: to give and to have
give-have.body: The second movement rests on two pairs: 與 and 有, to give and to have, and 人 and 己, others and self. Common sense makes them a scale: what goes to others leaves me. The lines join them the other way. Having given, one has more. The text does not rank self below others, and it does not say that having is bad; the words that end the two lines are 有 and 多, “has” and “much”. Giving needs a holder and a thing held, and [[the bellows|yu]] gives only because air comes in again. The passage does favor the open hand over [[the heap|ji]]. That corrects a world that measures a person by the store. It is not a rule to empty oneself. The favored side also turns: giving that keeps count is piling up by another road, and a giver who cannot receive leaves others no room to give. Where do you stand in that circle today?

lenses.ground: The passage has three movements and no images from nature at all; it is the plainest in the book. First, [[three mirror pairs|form]] about speech and knowledge: words [[to trust|xin]] against [[beautiful|mei]] words, the good against those who [[argue|bian]], those who know against the [[widely learned|bo]]. Second, three lines on having: the sage does not [[pile up|ji]]; [[having already worked for others|ji-yi]], has [[still more|yu]]; having given, has more again. Third, two last lines that set two ways side by side: heaven’s way [[benefits and does not harm|li]]; [[the sage’s way|sheng-dao]] acts and [[does not contend|bu-zheng]]. Inside the characters there is more to see: a person beside a word, two litigants with speech between them, a heap of grain, a blade that does not cut, and two hands that pull at one thing. In the received order this is [[the last passage|last-page]].
lenses.inner: The six opening lines are a mirror for the reader who has come to the end of a wise book. By now you have collected many fine sayings. You may be able to argue for them, and you know a good deal about the text. The passage looks at exactly these three gains, beauty, argument, and breadth, and says that none of them is the thing. What is left? [[Wang Bi’s three small notes|wb-one]] point to it: the plain stuff, the uncarved wood, the One. Then the lines on giving describe what a person is like who lives from there: nothing is stored up, [[not even insight|ji]]. An insight that is kept as a possession goes stale. Used for others, it [[comes back larger|yu]]. The last two words give the test for all of it: is there any pulling in this?
lenses.leading: The passage gives a leader three warnings and one rule. Distrust the polished report and the polished speaker; [[the words to rely on|xin]] are often clumsy. Notice who wins by argument in your meetings, because [[skill in argument|bian]] and being right are different gifts, and the age that prized debaters most was [[an age of ruin|debaters]]. Prefer the person who knows the work to the bottom over the one with [[a wide view of everything|bo]]. Then the rule: do not pile up. A leader has stores of several kinds: information, credit, access, the pleasant tasks. Each of them can grow when it is given away, and it often spoils when it is held. The closing pair gives the standard for every act of leading: it should benefit and not harm, and it should be done [[without a contest|bu-zheng]]. The collated silk text says that this is [[simply the human way|sheng-dao]].
lenses.body: 不爭 is a state of the body before it is a policy. [[爭|bu-zheng]] is two hands on one thing, each pulling. You can feel it without any opponent: one muscle pulls against another, the will pulls against the breath, the shoulders pull up while the mind says “relax”. Most effort that tires us is this inner tug. 為而不爭, to act and not contend, is movement in which nothing pulls against anything else: the push comes from the ground, passes through loose joints, and leaves through the hand. The lines on giving fit the breath. Lungs do not pile up. The out-breath that empties them fully is what lets the next breath come in by itself, and [[the bellows of passage 5|yu]] says the same. Breathe out to the end, once, and wait.
lenses.nature: The plainest words in the passage describe what the living world does every day. Nothing in a forest piles up for long. A tree that holds its leaves through winter in a cold country is broken by snow; the tree that gives them all to the ground is fed by them in spring. 既以與人，己愈多: having given, it has more. The sun is the largest case: it [[benefits and does not harm|li]], and it gives without a store that we can see the bottom of. A river that is dammed turns stale and fills with silt, and a river that runs stays itself. The granary is the human invention that set us apart from this, and the state grew from the granary. The passage does not ask us to burn the granary. It says that the sage does not live as one.
lenses.practice: As the last practice of the book, take one line from each movement. From the first: write or say [[one plain sentence|plain]] that you will stand beside, and let it be less handsome than you could make it. From the second: give one thing away completely, to the end, and do not replace it at once. Stay with the empty place for a day. From the third: do one piece of work today with no opponent in it at all, no rival, no deadline to beat, no earlier self to surpass. Act, and do not contend. Then close the book, as the passage itself advises: [[its words are fine|mei]], and fine words are not the point. If you open it again tomorrow, open it [[where the oldest copies begin|last-page]], or anywhere.

questions.claim: Words that can be trusted are not beautiful, and beautiful words are not to be trusted.
prompts: Do you agree? Think of the person whose word you rely on most. How do they speak?
Have fine words ever deceived you? Have you used them to cover something? What was covered?
Take the other side: beauty in speech is a kind of care, and a true thing that is well said reaches further. This book is itself well said. What does that do to the claim?
Do you distrust charm, or plainness? Where did that distrust begin, and whom has it kept out?

questions.claim: The one who stores nothing and gives to others ends with more, not less.
prompts: Has this been true for you in any sense that you can point to? Has it also been false?
What do you keep in reserve: money, time, affection, knowledge? What day are you keeping it for?
Now hold the opposite: what you give is gone, and a person with no store is at the mercy of others. That is also experience. Whose experience is it, in your family?
Are you easier with giving or with receiving? What does the harder one ask you to admit?

questions.claim: It is possible to act fully in the world and not compete with anyone.
prompts: Is it? Look at one piece of work that you did this week. Who was the rival in it, seen or unseen?
When did winning first matter to you, and what did you get for it?
Take the other side: contest sharpens people, and without a rival most of us do less than we can. What part of you needs the opponent?
If the contest stopped, what would move you to act? Does that question feel like rest, or like a threat?

plates.title: Two litigants and a word
plates.lesson: This is the largest character in the passage, and it is built in three columns. Cover the middle and you see the same shape twice: 辛 on the left and 辛 on the right. The Shuowen says that 辛 has to do with 辠, offence; modern scholars commonly explain the early character as a blade or chisel used to mark criminals and captives. Doubled, the two make 辡, and the Shuowen defines it: 辠人相與訟也, “accused persons who bring suit against each other”. Two parties stand face to face, each with a mark of guilt. Now look at what the scribes put between them. In our character it is 言, speech: 从言在辡之閒, “speech placed between the litigants”. That is 辯, to plead, to argue a case. The frame of two litigants was used again and again, and each time the thing in the middle changes the word. With 刂, a knife, in the middle it is 辨: to cut between two, to tell apart. With 力, strength, it is 辦: to deal with a matter; the Shuowen says “to apply strength”. With 糸, thread, it is 辮: to braid; the Shuowen says 交也, to cross over. With 瓜, a melon, it is 瓣: the Shuowen says the segments inside a melon, and now a petal. Speech, a knife, strength, thread, a fruit: something is always set between two sides. The line says that [[the good do not stand in that frame|bian]].
plates.brush: Twenty-one strokes: seven, seven, and seven. Each 辛 has a dot at the top, a level line, two small strokes that lean toward each other, two more level lines, and an upright. In the left-hand 辛 the last upright curves away to the lower left, to make room. In the right-hand 辛 it comes straight down and ends in a firm point. Between them, 言 is written second: a dot, a long level line, two shorter ones, and a small mouth in three strokes. The art is in the widths. Each column gets a third of the square, and each must be made narrow enough to share it; a beginner writes three full characters and the result sprawls. Keep the level lines of all three parts at different heights so that they do not form bars across the whole. In running script the two litigants shrink to a few quick turns.

plates.title: A person standing by a word
plates.lesson: Two parts, and the Shuowen calls their union 會意, joined meaning: 从人从言, “from a person and from speech”. On the left is 亻, the form that 人 takes at the side: a person seen in profile, two strokes. On the right is 言. The Shuowen separates 言 from its near neighbour: 直言曰言，論難曰語, “to speak straight out is 言; to discuss and dispute is 語”. The character has 口, a mouth, at its foot, and lines above it that are commonly explained as a tongue or a flute; the Shuowen names the upper part as a sound-mark. So 信 is a person, and straight speech. Nothing else is in the picture: no oath, no witness, no seal. Trust is only the nearness of the two. Look at the family of 言, which holds most of what people do with words: 語 (to discuss), 詩 (a poem; the Shuowen says 志也, what the heart is set on), 誠 (sincere; defined by 信, as 信 is defined by 誠), 訟 (a lawsuit), 說 (to explain), 謀 (to plan), 讓 (to yield). And [[辯|bian]], where speech stands between two opponents. In 信 it stands beside one person. The whole first movement of the passage is in that change of position. The word later came to mean a letter and then a message. Each is a word that still has its person beside it.
plates.brush: Nine strokes: two and seven. The person: a slash that falls to the lower left, and an upright that starts from the middle of the slash and stands straight. It is slim and tall, and it leans a little toward its partner. Then speech. A dot at the top, set above the centre of what is to come. A long level line, the widest stroke on the right side. Two shorter level lines under it, close together and of nearly equal length. Then the mouth: left side, top and right side with a corner, base. The mouth is no wider than the two short lines above it. The spaces between the four level strokes must be even; this is the test of the character. The upright of the person and the stack of level lines make the whole effect, and a good hand keeps the two parts close and does not let them touch.

plates.title: Two hands, one thing
plates.lesson: The last character of the book is a picture of a quarrel. The Shuowen’s definition is one word: 引也, “to pull”. It files the character under 𠬪, its sign for two hands, one that reaches down from above and one that reaches up from below. In the modern shape the upper hand is the claw-like top, 爫, which you know from 受, to receive, and 采, to pick. The lower hand is the part that looks like 彐, a hand seen from the side with three fingers. The long stroke that runs down through the lower hand is commonly explained as the thing between them, the object that both are holding. So: a hand, a hand, and one thing. In 受 two hands pass an object across, and the Shuowen defines it as handing over to one another. In 爭 the same two hands pull, and neither lets go. The two characters differ in what is between the hands, and in what the hands intend. The family of 爭 holds a surprise. 靜, stillness, the great word of passage 16, has 爭 on its right side as its sound-part; so has 淨, clean. The Shuowen treats this as sound alone, and no one should build a theory on it. Still, each time the book wrote “stillness” it wrote a quarrel beside the colour of new growth, 青. The final words are [[不爭|bu-zheng]]: the hands open, and the thing between them is free.
plates.brush: Eight strokes. The upper hand takes four: a short flat slash across the top, written from right to left; two dots under it, side by side; and a longer slash that falls to the left. Then the lower hand. Stroke five is a level line that turns a corner and comes down a short way. Stroke six is a long level line that passes right through and reaches out on both sides; it is the widest stroke and the balance beam of the character. Stroke seven is a short level line below it, which closes the hand. Stroke eight is the upright: it starts inside the hand, runs straight down through all the level lines, and ends in a hook to the left. Write it last and without hurry. It is the thing that the two hands hold, and, in the received order, the last stroke of the whole book.
